item.text: [{"taxonId":1599165,"summary":"A shrubby hybrid rose of cultivated Dutch origin, developed between the 17th and 19th centuries, possibly earlier. Its highly scented flowers are round and densely packed with thin overlapping petals, usually pink but sometimes white or dark red-purple.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p6"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":1611056,"summary":"A citrus tree whose wild form evolved in a restricted region of southern China and Vietnam. Its small, flattened fruits have thin, loose, pebbly skin and separate easily into segments; most commercial strains are sweeter than the bitter ancestral mandarin.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Fruit is eaten fresh or used in salads, desserts and main dishes; peel is used fresh, as zest, dried, or as flavouring.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p3","s1:p15"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p25","s1:p26"]}},{"taxonId":1628098,"summary":"An evergreen shrub or small tree of cultivated west Pacific origin, created by Polynesians from parent species originating in Vanuatu and French Polynesia. Its typically red, five-petalled flowers have prominent orange-tipped structures, while cultivated forms range from white and yellow to blue and purple and may be double-flowered.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Flowers are eaten in salads in the Pacific Islands and are dried for beverages in several countries.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p3","s1:p5","s1:p7","s1:p13"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p21"]}},{"taxonId":1639001,"summary":"A rosette-forming flowering plant endemic to Puebla and Oaxaca, Mexico. Its thick, pointed oval leaves are olive, grey or whitish green with red-brown markings, and its late-spring flowers are scarlet with yellow tips.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":1645811,"summary":"A grass native to the Pyrenees of France and Spain, Portugal and Morocco. It is the only species in its genus and has blunt to squared-off outer flower bracts, with florets about half their length.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p3"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":1656026,"summary":"A genus of four grass species native to Mediterranean Europe, North Africa and western Asia from the Levant to Turkmenistan.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":1687652,"summary":"An annual or perennial herb or woody-based subshrub, likely native to West Africa. Its pale flowers have a dark red spot, while the calyx becomes fleshy and deep crimson as the fruit matures. The calyces are commonly steeped for an infusion, and the stems yield fibre.","humanEdibility":"yes","edibilityNote":"Leaves, young stems and fruits are cooked; calyces and fruits make drinks, and the fruits can be made into jam.","evidence":{"summary":["s1:p2","s1:p3","s1:p4"],"humanEdibility":["s1:p10","s1:p12","s1:p16","s1:p21"]}},{"taxonId":67900,"summary":"A moss of unstated native origin, frequently recorded at numerous Algerian localities, including Algiers, Kabylie, Constantine and Tlemcen.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":67907,"summary":"A moss of unstated native origin, commonly recorded across numerous Algerian localities and settings, from Skikda beach to mountain forests.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1"],"humanEdibility":[]}},{"taxonId":67917,"summary":"A moss of unstated native origin, widespread in Europe and also reported from parts of Asia, the Americas and Tristan da Cunha, but rare around the Mediterranean. It usually grows in acidic forests on soil near tree bases, sheltered banks or rocks. In Tunisia it was sterile and confined to a tiny patch in the Oued Zen Valley.","humanEdibility":"unknown","edibilityNote":null,"evidence":{"summary":["s1:p1","s1:p2","s1:p3"],"humanEdibility":[]}}]
